title: Build and Benchmark a Quantum Algorithm
summary: Implement a quantum algorithm end-to-end (Grover, VQE, or QAOA), run it on simulator + real hardware, characterize noise, apply error mitigation, compare to classical baseline.
contentIntro:
## What you'll build

One quantum algorithm taken end-to-end: theoretical analysis, simulator implementation, real-hardware execution, noise characterization, error mitigation, classical-baseline comparison.

This capstone is the synthesis of the quantum-engineer path. It exercises everything: gate-level circuits, simulators, hardware, NISQ noise, classical comparisons.

## What you'll demonstrate

- You can implement a quantum algorithm in Qiskit / Cirq / PennyLane.
- You can analyze its theoretical speedup + practical limits.
- You can run on real quantum hardware (IBM Quantum, IonQ, etc.) — free tiers available.
- You can characterize hardware noise + apply error mitigation.
- You can produce a defended report comparing quantum vs classical performance.
contentUndergrad:
## Why this capstone

Most quantum-computing learning is theoretical. Real quantum work involves: circuit compilation, hardware noise, mitigation, and honest classical comparisons. This capstone forces you to do all of it.

By the end you have one full quantum-algorithm artifact: working code, simulator + real-hardware results, noise analysis, classical comparison, defended report. Portfolio-worthy.

## Algorithm choices

Pick one (or propose another with author approval):

**A: Grover's search**:
- Implement Grover for a small problem (5-10 qubits).
- Test on simulator + real hardware.
- Compare classical search vs quantum at the achievable scale.
- Demonstrate quadratic-speedup mechanism (despite no actual advantage at small scale).

**B: VQE for H₂ or LiH**:
- Encode the molecular Hamiltonian.
- Implement hardware-efficient or UCC ansatz.
- Run VQE on simulator + real hardware.
- Compare against classical CCSD or full CI.

**C: QAOA for MaxCut**:
- Pick a small graph (8-15 nodes).
- Implement QAOA at p=1, p=2, p=3.
- Run on simulator + real hardware.
- Compare against Goemans-Williamson + simulated annealing.

## Hardware access

Free tier options:
- **IBM Quantum Experience** (free tier): up to 127 qubits.
- **IonQ Cloud** via AWS Braket: limited free credits.
- **Quantinuum** via cloud: trial access.
- **PennyLane** with cloud backends: convenient interface.

Local simulation works for any milestone; hardware access is required for milestones 4-5.

## Pacing

6 weeks at ~5-8 hrs/week. Most time: milestones 3 (real-hardware execution) + 5 (noise + mitigation). Milestones 1-2 are setup.

## Tools

- **Qiskit** (Python, IBM ecosystem): standard.
- **Cirq** (Python, Google): alternative.
- **PennyLane** (Python, hardware-agnostic): convenient.
- **Q#** (.NET, Microsoft): for Microsoft Azure Quantum.
- **NumPy + SciPy**: classical baselines.
contentGrad:
## Notes for the experienced

If you've worked with quantum hardware professionally, the value is the **rigorous benchmarking + honest reporting**. Many published quantum demos are subtly cherry-picked. The rubric specifically rewards honest classical comparison + acknowledgment of limitations.

Likely places where quantum researchers cut corners:
- Cherry-picked classical baselines.
- Insufficient noise characterization on real hardware.
- Overstating advantage from small-scale demos.
- Missing post-selection + measurement-error effects.

## Variants

- **Quantum-supremacy variant**: implement a small random-circuit-sampling experiment; estimate classical-simulation cost.
- **QML variant**: train a variational quantum classifier on a small dataset (Iris, MNIST 4-classes).
- **Quantum simulation variant**: simulate a small lattice model (Ising, Hubbard).
- **Quantum chemistry variant**: VQE for a small molecule beyond H₂.

Author approval required.

milestones.title: Algorithm choice + theoretical analysis
milestones.description:
Pick your algorithm. Write down: theoretical speedup vs classical, problem size, expected behavior, success criteria. Implement a tiny version on simulator (3-5 qubits) to verify understanding.

**Deliverables**: a `theory.md` writeup analyzing the algorithm + an initial Qiskit/Cirq notebook running it on a small problem.

milestones.title: Simulator implementation + scaling
milestones.description:
Scale up to the largest size that's classically simulable (10-25 qubits typical). Run the algorithm without noise (statevector simulator). Verify scaling matches theoretical predictions.

**Deliverables**: cleaned-up implementation + a `simulator.md` writeup with scaling results.

milestones.title: Real-hardware execution
milestones.description:
Run the algorithm on real quantum hardware (IBM Quantum, IonQ, etc.). Pick a problem size that fits real-hardware noise budget (typically much smaller than simulator). Document: hardware platform, qubit selection, gate-error rates, coherence times.

**Deliverables**: real-hardware results + a `hardware.md` writeup describing setup + observed performance.

milestones.title: Noise characterization
milestones.description:
Characterize the noise affecting your hardware execution. Measure: gate fidelities (via randomized benchmarking or process tomography), coherence times (T₁, T₂), readout errors. Quantify how much each noise source affects your algorithm's success rate.

**Deliverables**: characterization data + a `noise.md` writeup attributing observed errors to specific sources.

milestones.title: Error mitigation
milestones.description:
Apply at least two error-mitigation techniques: readout error mitigation + zero-noise extrapolation (or similar). Quantify the improvement.

**Deliverables**: mitigation code + a `mitigation.md` writeup with before/after comparisons.

milestones.title: Classical baseline + final report
milestones.description:
Implement a strong classical baseline for the same problem. Compare runtimes + accuracy honestly. Write the final defense report: theoretical speedup vs practical advantage, hardware noise as the dominant constraint, path to potential future advantage.

**Deliverables**: classical baseline code + a `defense.md` (~1500 words) covering theoretical, simulator, hardware, mitigation, classical-comparison results + an honest assessment of where the field is.
